--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON) ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Build** an activity-on-node (AON) network from a precedence table. 2. **Apply** the rules for constructing a valid network diagram. 3. **Perform** the forward pass to find early start (ES) and early finish (EF). 4. **Perform** the backward pass to find late start (LS) and late finish (LF). 5. **Calculate** total float and identify the **critical path**. 6. **Compute** a three-point (PERT) activity duration. 7. **Choose** a strategy to shorten the critical path when the project is too long.
Before we begin: which task can slip without moving the deadline? On any project some tasks have slack and some do not. Guessing wrong --- pouring effort into a task with float while a zero-float task quietly slips --- is one of the most common ways schedules die. The network diagram tells you which is which.
## Introduction: when can we launch? The RC-vehicle WBS gives you a list of activities and their durations. It does *not* tell you how long the whole project takes, because the activities are not all independent --- you cannot assemble a prototype before the body is designed. A **network diagram** captures those dependencies and answers the question the sponsor actually cares about: **what is the earliest the project can finish, and which activities decide that date?** ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** Every automotive program plan is a critical-path network: the "job one" date is the length of the longest dependent chain. A food-plant commissioning schedule uses the same math to decide whether sanitation qualification can overlap controls checkout. A defense contractor reports critical-path status to the customer monthly --- slipping a critical task is a contractual event. :::
## From WBS to precedence table For each activity you need its **duration** and its **immediate predecessors** --- the activities that must finish before it can start. Rules for a valid AON network: 1. Determine precedence ordering **before** drawing. 2. Networks flow **left to right**. 3. An activity cannot begin until **all** connected predecessors are complete. 4. Arrows show **precedence and logical flow** (they may cross, but minimize it). 5. Every activity has a **unique identifier**. 6. **No looping** back to an earlier activity. 7. It is common (not required) to start from a **single start node**... 8. ...and end at a **single end node**. ## AON node anatomy Each activity is a box with six numbers: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The six-number activity node. Forward pass fills the top row (ES, DUR, EF); backward pass fills the bottom (LS, FLT, LF).](06-Network-Diagrams-and-AON_files/figure-epub/fig-node-anatomy-06-1.png){#fig-node-anatomy-06 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: An activity with 2+ predecessors flowing **in** is a **merge**; one with 2+ successors flowing **out** is a **burst**. ## Worked Example: the RC-vehicle sub-project network Ten activities (a simplified slice of the project): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acts <- data.frame( id = LETTERS[1:10], dur = c(5, 8, 3, 4, 5, 7, 6, 8, 6, 5), pred = c("", "A", "B", "A", "C", "C", "D,E", "F", "G", "H,I"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) knitr::kable(acts, col.names = c("Activity", "Duration (days)", "Predecessors"), align = c("c", "c", "l")) |> kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Activity Duration (days) Predecessors
A 5
B 8 A
C 3 B
D 4 A
E 5 C
F 7 C
G 6 D,E
H 8 F
I 6 G
J 5 H,I
````` ::: ::: ### Forward pass (ES, EF) Move left to right. $EF = ES + DUR$. Carry each EF forward as the successor's ES --- **except at a merge, where the ES is the largest incoming EF.** ### Backward pass (LS, LF) Move right to left from the project finish. $LS = LF - DUR$. Carry each LS back as the predecessor's LF --- **except at a burst, where the LF is the smallest outgoing LS.** ### Float and the critical path $$FLT = LS - ES = LF - EF$$ Activities with **zero float** cannot slip without delaying the whole project --- together they form the **critical path**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # A small critical-path solver (base R + data.frame). cpm <- function(df) { df$pred <- strsplit(df$pred, ",") n <- nrow(df); id <- df$id ES <- EF <- LS <- LF <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, n), id) # Forward pass (ids are already in a valid topological order here) for (i in seq_len(n)) { p <- df$pred[[i]]; p <- p[p != ""] ES[i] <- if (length(p) == 0) 0 else max(EF[p]) EF[i] <- ES[i] + df$dur[i] } proj <- max(EF) # Backward pass for (i in rev(seq_len(n))) { succ <- id[sapply(df$pred, function(pp) id[i] %in% pp)] LF[i] <- if (length(succ) == 0) proj else min(LS[succ]) LS[i] <- LF[i] - df$dur[i] } data.frame(Activity = id, Dur = df$dur, ES = ES, EF = EF, LS = LS, LF = LF, Float = LS - ES, Critical = ifelse(LS - ES == 0, " <- critical", "")) } res <- cpm(acts) print(res, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nProject duration: %d days\n", max(res$EF))) cat("Critical path:", paste(res$Activity[res$Float == 0], collapse = " - "), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Activity Dur ES EF LS LF Float Critical A 5 0 5 0 5 0 <- critical B 8 5 13 5 13 0 <- critical C 3 13 16 13 16 0 <- critical D 4 5 9 17 21 12 E 5 16 21 16 21 0 <- critical F 7 16 23 18 25 2 G 6 21 27 21 27 0 <- critical H 8 23 31 25 33 2 I 6 27 33 27 33 0 <- critical J 5 33 38 33 38 0 <- critical Project duration: 38 days Critical path: A - B - C - E - G - I - J ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Total float per activity. The zero-float bars (A, B, C, E, G, I, J) are the critical path; D has 12 days of slack, F and H have 2.](06-Network-Diagrams-and-AON_files/figure-epub/fig-cpm-float-06-1.png){#fig-cpm-float-06 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The whole forward/backward/float sequence is one connected calculation --- change any duration and every downstream number moves --- so work it as a block, not as isolated steps. ## Three-point (PERT) duration estimates When a duration is uncertain, estimate three values --- **optimistic** $o$, **most likely** $m$, **pessimistic** $p$ --- and combine them: $$t_e = \frac{o + 4m + p}{6}$$ ### Try it yourself: PERT durations ```{webr-r} #| label: pert-te-06 tasks <- data.frame( id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"), o = c(12, 7, 15, 9, 24), m = c(15, 10, 19, 13, 26), p = c(17, 13, 23, 16, 30) ) tasks$te <- round((tasks$o + 4 * tasks$m + tasks$p) / 6, 2) tasks$sd <- round((tasks$p - tasks$o) / 6, 2) # activity standard deviation print(tasks, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nSum of expected durations along this chain: %.2f days\n", sum(tasks$te))) ```
Why the weight of 4 on the most-likely value? PERT assumes each activity duration follows a Beta distribution skewed toward the most-likely value, with the optimistic and pessimistic values as the tails. Weighting $m$ by 4 and $o$, $p$ by 1 each (dividing by 6) is the standard approximation of that distribution's mean. The activity standard deviation $(p - o)/6$ becomes important in [Chapter 8](08-Project-Scheduling.qmd), where you combine them to find the probability of finishing on time.
## Shortening the critical path Only work on the **critical path** shortens the project. Options, roughly in order of preference: 1. **Eliminate** critical tasks (is it truly needed?). 2. **Re-plan series paths to run in parallel.** 3. **Overlap** sequential tasks (start the successor before the predecessor fully finishes --- *fast-tracking*). 4. **Shorten durations on critical activities** --- prefer earlier-starting tasks, then the longest, then the easiest, then the ones **cheapest to speed up**. ### Try it yourself: recompute the critical path after a change ```{webr-r} #| label: path-duration-06 # All start-to-finish paths through the sub-project network, with activity durations. dur <- c(A = 5, B = 8, C = 3, D = 4, E = 5, F = 7, G = 6, H = 8, I = 6, J = 5) paths <- list( "A-B-C-E-G-I-J" = c("A","B","C","E","G","I","J"), "A-B-C-F-H-J" = c("A","B","C","F","H","J"), "A-D-G-I-J" = c("A","D","G","I","J") ) path_len <- sapply(paths, function(p) sum(dur[p])) cat("Baseline path lengths:\n"); print(path_len) cat(sprintf("Critical path: %s (%d days)\n\n", names(which.max(path_len)), max(path_len))) # Now crash B from 8 to 5 days and re-check: dur["B"] <- 5 path_len2 <- sapply(paths, function(p) sum(dur[p])) cat("After crashing B by 3 days:\n"); print(path_len2) cat(sprintf("New critical path: %s (%d days)\n", names(which.max(path_len2)), max(path_len2))) cat("Note how the critical path can *shift* to a different chain once you crash enough.\n") ``` ## The downside of network diagrams - Often **not drawn to scale** --- time is just a number, which can create a false sense of how much time is available. - Can be **too large and complex** to be useful. - **Faulty construction logic** can oversimplify or misrepresent the work. - Sometimes used for work they do not suit. - **Positive bias** creeps into PERT estimates (people are optimistic). ## Key Takeaways - Build the **AON network** from a precedence table (durations + immediate predecessors); it flows left to right with no loops. - **Forward pass**: $EF = ES + DUR$; at a **merge**, ES = the largest incoming EF. Gives the **project duration**. - **Backward pass**: $LS = LF - DUR$; at a **burst**, LF = the smallest outgoing LS. - **Float** $= LS - ES = LF - EF$. **Zero-float** activities form the **critical path** --- the longest dependent chain, and the only one worth shortening. - **PERT**: $t_e = (o + 4m + p)/6$, activity SD $= (p - o)/6$. - Shorten the critical path by **eliminating, parallelizing, overlapping, or crashing** critical tasks --- and re-check, because the critical path can shift. ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Solve this network | Activity | Predecessors | Duration | |---|---|---| | A | none | 3 | | B | A | 4 | | C | A | 2 | | D | B | 5 | | E | C | 1 | | F | E | 2 | | G | D, E | 4 | | H | F, G | 3 | | I | H | 6 | Find the project duration and the critical path. **Solution.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- data.frame( id = LETTERS[1:9], dur = c(3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 2, 4, 3, 6), pred = c("", "A", "A", "B", "C", "E", "D,E", "F,G", "H"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) r1 <- cpm(p1) # reuse the solver defined earlier in this chapter print(r1, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nProject duration: %d days\n", max(r1$EF))) cat("Critical path:", paste(r1$Activity[r1$Float == 0], collapse = " - "), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Activity Dur ES EF LS LF Float Critical A 3 0 3 0 3 0 <- critical B 4 3 7 3 7 0 <- critical C 2 3 5 9 11 6 D 5 7 12 7 12 0 <- critical E 1 5 6 11 12 6 F 2 6 8 14 16 8 G 4 12 16 12 16 0 <- critical H 3 16 19 16 19 0 <- critical I 6 19 25 19 25 0 <- critical Project duration: 25 days Critical path: A - B - D - G - H - I ``` ::: ::: Duration 25 days; critical path A--B--D--G--H--I. (The chain A--B--D--G is what pushes E, F, and C off the critical path --- D's 5 days arriving at the G merge beat E's early finish by 6 days.)
Problem 2: PERT and the optimistic tail An activity is estimated at $o = 6$, $m = 9$, $p = 24$ days. (a) What is $t_e$? (b) Why is $t_e$ noticeably larger than $m$? (c) What is the activity standard deviation? **Solution.** (a) $t_e = (6 + 36 + 24)/6 = 11$ days. (b) The pessimistic tail is far from the most-likely value (24 vs 9) while the optimistic tail is close (6 vs 9), so the distribution is **right-skewed** and its mean sits above $m$. (c) SD $= (24 - 6)/6 = 3$ days --- a wide, risky activity.
Problem 3 (discussion): which task do you crash? On the sub-project network, the critical path is A--B--C--E--G--I--J (38 days) and the sponsor needs 34. Crash data: B costs \$500/day to shorten (max 3 days), G costs \$1 200/day (max 2 days), E costs \$300/day (max 2 days). Which combination gets you to 34 days at least cost, and what do you check afterward? **Discussion points.** You need 4 days. Cheapest first: E for 2 days (\$600), then B for 2 days (\$1 000) --- total \$1 600 for 4 days. Avoid G at \$1 200/day. **Then re-run the network**: after removing 4 days from this chain, another path (e.g. A--B--C--F--H--J) may now be critical or co-critical, and crashing further would have to shorten *both*.
